title: Python Environments: venv, pip, and Pinned Dependencies
intro: Python is the default language for automation: cloud SDKs, CI glue, data clean-up. Most trouble with it isn't the code, it's which Python and which packages a script actually ran with. You're in a repository containing a script, rotate_keys.py, and a requirements.txt.

steps.prompt: Create a virtual environment in the directory .venv.
steps.explanation: A private copy of the interpreter's package directory, just for this project.
steps.why: Without one, 'pip install' goes into the system Python, where one project's packages overwrite another's and can break tools the operating system itself depends on. Recent distributions refuse outright ('externally-managed-environment'). One environment per project is the rule; add .venv to .gitignore.

steps.explanation: The prompt shows the environment; 'python' and 'pip' now mean the ones inside .venv.
steps.why: Activating only puts .venv/bin first on PATH. Nothing more. So scripts, cron jobs, and systemd units don't need to activate anything: they call .venv/bin/python by its full path. That's also the fix when a job 'can't find a module' that works in your shell.

steps.prompt: Install the project's dependencies from requirements.txt.
steps.fake_output:
Collecting boto3==1.35.20
Collecting requests==2.32.3
Installing collected packages: urllib3, jmespath, botocore, s3transfer, boto3, certifi, idna, charset-normalizer, requests
Successfully installed boto3-1.35.20 requests-2.32.3 ...
steps.explanation: The exact versions listed in the file, plus what they depend on.
steps.why: 'python -m pip' guarantees you're using the pip that belongs to the python you're running; a bare 'pip' can be a different installation's. The '==' pins are what make this repeatable: the same file gives the same packages next month. Unpinned requirements are how a script that worked on Friday breaks on Monday with no code change (scripting-incident-001).

steps.prompt: Record exactly what's installed now, including indirect dependencies, into requirements.txt.
steps.fake_output:
(no output: requirements.txt written)

requests==2.32.3

steps.explanation: Every package, direct and indirect, with its exact version.
steps.why: The indirect ones matter most: you never chose urllib3, and a new major version of it is what breaks you. freeze is the simple way to lock them. The better way keeps two files: your direct dependencies in requirements.in, and a compiled, fully pinned requirements.txt generated by pip-compile or uv, so upgrades are a deliberate, reviewable diff.

steps.prompt: Check which installed packages have newer versions available.
steps.fake_output:
Package    Version   Latest    Type
---------- --------- --------- -----
boto3      1.35.20   1.35.31   wheel
botocore   1.35.20   1.35.31   wheel
urllib3    2.2.3     2.3.0     wheel
steps.why: Pinning doesn't mean never upgrading; it means upgrading on purpose. Let a bot propose these (Renovate or Dependabot, cicd-tutorial-019) and let the tests decide. For command-line tools you just want to use, such as ansible or httpie, 'pipx install' gives each its own environment so they can't conflict with your projects.
